newsitem.title: USA: House votes to free population aid funds.
newsitem.headline: House votes to free population aid funds.

text.p: The House of Representatives voted narrowly on Thursday to speed up U.S. international family planning aid, rebuffing a campaign against the measure by anti-abortion forces.
The 220-209 vote marked a victory for the Clinton administration in the first abortion debate of the new Congress by allowing aid to go ahead without abortion restrictions.

In a separate action, the House sought to have it both ways by approving, 231-194, a bill that would revive abortion-related restrictions in effect during the Reagan and Bush administrations. However, this measure is almost certain to die either in the Senate or under a presidential veto.

"This is the first time in three years that the House of Representatives has chosen to support international family planning efforts without the simultaneous imposition of abortion-related restrictions," said Dr. Nils Daulaire, senior health policy adviser at the Agency for International Development.
He called the action "a real sea change."
The separate bill would link the aid with reimposition of a policy of denying funds for population groups that perform or advocate abortion, even if they use their own money for that purpose.
President Bill Clinton scrapped this policy of his Republican predecessors shortly after taking office.
The twin House votes followed replays of numerous past debates on U.S. aid for international family planning. Organisations on both sides of the issue had been pouring out statements for some time.
A dispute last year led to a compromise agreement under which Congress voted to appropriate $385 million in aid for the current fiscal year but delay disbursement until July 1.

But the agreement allowed the aid to start on March 1 if Clinton found the restriction was having a negative impact on population programmes -- a finding he has made -- and if both houses of Congress approved a joint resolution to that effect.
The House-passed resolution now goes to the Senate, which must act before Feb. 28. It will not take up the issue until it returns on Feb. 25 from a week-long recess.

The bill reimposing the abortion restrictions was proposed by anti-abortion activist Christopher Smith, a New Jersey Republican who had argued strongly against passage of the first measure, calling it "strongly pro-abortion in its effect -- fat payday for abortion providers."
Smith said the debate marked "the beginning of a long fight" on the issue in the new Congress.
Illinois Republican Henry Hyde declared the issue "is not about family planning -- this is about abortion."
Supporters of the resolution cited exploding populations in undeveloped countries leading to environmental degradation, famine and export of American jobs to low-wage countries.
"We must not hold the poor children of the world hostage to congressional politics," Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, said.

Representative Tony Hall, an Ohio Democrat, who described himself as pro-life, said anti-abortion forces had gone too far by making release of the funds a "pro-life" issue. "Pro-life forces have done great damage to poor communities all over the world," Hall said.

Under legislation triggered by the administration-backed resolution monthly payouts would be limited to a maximum of 8 percent -- meaning that only $215 million of the $385 million appropriation could be spent by the end of the fiscal year. Smith's bill would remove these limits.
